what_it_does: Floorplanning is an early step in chip design where engineers decide where to place large functional blocks (CPU cores, memory banks, etc.) on a silicon die; a bad initial arrangement leads to longer wires, more power use, and slower chips. Classical automated floorplanners are sensitive to where they start — a poor starting guess leads to poor results — while machine-learning approaches can find good solutions but are slow and computationally expensive. This paper proposes using a diffusion model (the same class of generative AI used in image synthesis, which learns to gradually refine random noise into a structured output) to generate high-quality starting floorplans. A heterogeneous graph neural network (a type of AI that processes relationships between different kinds of objects, here both blocks and their pin connections) guides the diffusion process so it understands the circuit's connectivity. A custom sampling function steers the generation toward layouts with shorter total wire length and less overlap between blocks. The abstract is a late-breaking result (a short preliminary report), so full experimental comparisons are not yet available.
